title: Instrument Junction Box: 9 Smart Rules for Safe Wiring
text:
Design

 Instrument Junction Box: 9 Smart Rules for Safe Wiring

 Every field transmitter, switch and valve signal passes through a junction box before it reaches the control room. A well designed box keeps those signals safe, dry, segregated and easy to trace for the whole life of the plant.

 
 Single and Multi Pair 
 Terminal Sizing 
 IS Segregation 
 Ex e and Ex d 
 




 A junction box looks like a simple steel enclosure, yet poor design causes water ingress, noise, wrong wiring and hazardous area failures. This guide covers the practical rules for designing and specifying one correctly.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how an instrument junction box is designed, from terminal sizing and spares to IS segregation, Ex protection, IP rating, glands and the JB schedule.


 
 
 
 What Is an Instrument Junction Box?


 An instrument junction box is a field enclosure where the individual cables from several instruments are terminated and joined to one multicore cable that runs to the control room. It reduces the number of long cables, keeps terminations protected and gives a convenient point for testing and fault finding.


 In a typical plant, the field JB sits between the instruments and the marshalling cabinet . From there the signals go to the DCS, PLC or safety system input cards.


 
 
 Image credit: Control and Instrumentation . Photo courtesy of Control and Instrumentation, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 The same box idea is used for analog loops, digital signals, thermocouples, fieldbus spurs and power to solenoids. How the cables are routed from the field to the system is shown in PLC wiring from field instrument to system cabinet .


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Single Pair and Multi Pair Instrument Junction Box Types


 
 Single Pair JB
 Terminates one instrument cable, often for a splice or a remote device.
 Best for: long runs, isolated instruments
 Simple 

 Multi Pair JB
 Collects 6 to 48 or more field pairs onto one or two multicore cables.
 Best for: process units with many instruments
 Most Common 

 Fieldbus or Power JB
 Holds device couplers, spur protection or solenoid power terminals.
 Best for: Foundation Fieldbus, Profibus PA, valve power
 Special 




 Each multicore pair carries one loop, such as a 4 to 20 mA current loop , with an overall shield and often an individual shield per pair. Thermocouple extension cables need their own JB with compensating terminals.


 Do You Know?
 Many specifications ask for multicore cables with two or more unused pairs left for future use. Control and Instrumentation recommends this so new instruments can be added without pulling a new cable.



 9 Design Rules for an Instrument Junction Box


 
 1
 Group by Signal
 Keep analog, digital, power and fieldbus in separate boxes.


 2
 Segregate IS
 Never mix IS and non IS circuits in the same box without approved separation.


 3
 Match the Area
 Select Ex e, Ex d or Ex i suitable for the zone, gas group and T class.


 4
 Pick IP Rating
 Use IP56 or better outdoors, higher for washdown.


 5
 Choose Material
 SS316L or GRP for outdoor and corrosive sites.


 6
 Size Terminals
 Allow for all cores, shields and the spare margin.


 7
 Plan Entries
 Bottom entry glands, certified and with plugs on unused holes.


 8
 Earth Properly
 Provide earth studs and isolated shield bars.


 9
 Label Clearly
 Tag the box, terminals and cores to match the JB schedule.





 Quick Tip
 Mount the box so that all glands enter from the bottom. Top entry glands collect rainwater and are the most common cause of water inside a JB.



 Terminal Sizing and Spare Philosophy


 When sizing an instrument junction box, count the terminals for every core, then add separate terminals for each pair shield and the overall shield. A 3 wire RTD or a 4 wire loop needs more terminals than a 2 wire transmitter, so read the instrument list carefully.


 Most projects keep about 10 to 20 percent spare terminals and spare multicore pairs, as specified by the client. Spare cores should be terminated on spare terminals and labelled, not left loose inside the box.


 
 Used terminals = Instruments × Terminals per loop 
 Spare terminals = Used terminals × Spare % ÷ 100 
 Multicore pairs ≥ Instruments × (1 + Spare % ÷ 100) 

Example:
20 transmitters, 3 terminals each (plus, minus, shield), 20 percent spare
Used = 20 × 3 = 60, spare = 60 × 20 ÷ 100 = 12
 Total terminals = 72, multicore pairs at least 24 



 Choose terminals rated for the conductor size, usually 1.5 or 2.5 square mm for signals. Disconnect or knife terminals on loops help testing without lifting wires, and fused terminals suit solenoid power.

 Second Worked Example: Mixed Signal Area


 A compressor skid has 14 transmitters with 3 terminals each and 6 RTDs with 4 terminals each, and the client wants 15 percent spare. Used terminals are 14 × 3 plus 6 × 4, which is 66, and the spare is 66 × 0.15, rounded up to 10.


 The box therefore needs at least 76 signal terminals, plus end stops, earth bar and markers. The multicore needs at least 20 × 1.15, rounded up to 23 pairs, so the next standard 24 pair cable is chosen.
